Why NFL Spreads Carry a .5 "Hook" at 3 and 7 — and When Books Drop It

Published October 5, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Open an NFL odds board on a Sunday morning and you'll see very few whole-number spreads. Instead of a tidy "Bills -3," you'll usually find "Bills -2.5" or "Bills -3.5." That extra half-point, commonly called a hook, isn't decoration and it isn't random. It's a sportsbook's answer to a specific mathematical problem — what to do with the single most common margin of victory in football — and the direction a book hooks the line tells you something real about which side of a game is getting more public and sharp money.

The push problem a whole number creates

A spread bet settles in one of three ways: you win, you lose, or — if the final margin lands exactly on the number — you push, and your stake is simply returned. Sportsbooks generally dislike pushes. A push means the book collected money, held it for a few hours, and gave it back without ever getting to keep the vig on that side of the market. It's not catastrophic, but across tens of thousands of tickets a week, a book that structures its biggest markets to push constantly is leaving money on the table it could otherwise hold.

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple: shade the number off the whole integer. If the "true" market view of a game is that one team is a 3-point favorite, pricing it at exactly -3 invites a push whenever the game ends on that number — which, as the next section explains, happens a lot in the NFL. Price it at -2.5 or -3.5 instead, and a push becomes mathematically impossible. Every ticket resolves win or lose, and the book collects its vig on whichever side wins. That's the entire logic of the hook in one sentence: it's a push-elimination tool, not a reflection of some precise half-point of extra information about the matchup.

Why 3 and 7 specifically need the hook

Not every number needs this treatment equally, because final margins in NFL games aren't spread evenly across all possible scores. A field goal (3 points) and a touchdown with the extra point (7 points) are the two single scoring plays that most directly decide a close game, so games end with a final margin of exactly 3 or exactly 7 far more often than they end on, say, 4, 5, 9, or 11. Books and sharp bettors alike have tracked this clustering for decades; it's the same clustering that makes 3 and 7 the "key numbers" referenced constantly in spread and teaser strategy. Because so much probability mass sits on those two specific integers, a whole-number line at 3 or 7 would push dramatically more often than a whole-number line at almost any other value — which is exactly why you almost never see a flat "-3" or "-7" sit on a board for long once real money starts flowing in.

Other numbers get hooked too, just with lower stakes attached. A line near 6 might carry a half-point because 6 also shows up somewhat more than its neighbors (two field goals), but the effect is far weaker than at 3 and 7, so you'll more often see whole numbers survive away from the two headline key numbers.

Which way a book hooks the line, and what it signals

Once a book has decided a game is close to a key number, it still has to choose which side of that number to land on, and that choice is informative. If early money and model projections point to a true 3-point favorite, a book might open at -2.5 to make the favorite's side marginally easier to clear, inviting more favorite money and totals balance, or it might open at -3.5 if it wants to lean the other way and encourage underdog action. As real bets come in, the book can also move the hook itself — shifting a line from -2.5 to -3.5 crosses the key number 3 entirely, which is a much bigger deal than a move from -6.5 to -7.5 that stays on the same side of a key number but simply slides further from it.

Watching which direction a line hooks, and whether it later crosses the key number altogether, is one of the more reliable free signals in line-watching — it tells you where the book believes real risk is concentrated, separate from whatever a given handicapper's model says about the matchup itself.

Line moveWhat it means
-2.5 to -3.5Crosses the key number 3 — a meaningful shift in who needs what to win or push-proof the book
-3.5 to -4.5Moves away from 3 without crossing it — smaller practical impact on outcomes
+6.5 to +7.5Crosses the key number 7 — now a backdoor touchdown cover changes outcomes it previously didn't
-9.5 to -10.5Moves between two non-key numbers — mostly a vig/liability adjustment, lower strategic weight

A worked example: the cost of being on the wrong side of a hook

Say the home favorite opens at -3.5. You bet the favorite, expecting a comfortable win. The game ends 20-17 — a 3-point win. On a flat -3 line, that's a push and you get your stake back. On -3.5, you lose the bet outright, because the favorite needed to win by at least 4. That half-point, worth nothing in the vast majority of games that end on some other margin, is worth your entire stake in exactly the scenario — a 3-point final margin — that happens more often than almost any other outcome in football. This is the real, concrete cost of a hook landing against you, and it's also the exact reason buying a half-point off a key number (paying extra vig to move from -3.5 to -3, or from -3 to -2.5) is one of the few "buy the point" situations experienced bettors consistently say is worth the price, specifically at 3 and, to a slightly lesser extent, 7.

Takeaway: A hook isn't a prediction about the final score — it's a sportsbook's way of refusing to let the most common NFL margins turn into a free push. Whether that hook sits for you or against you is often decided by which side of 3 or 7 the closing number lands on, not by anything unique to that week's matchup.

Where hooks barely matter

Away from 3 and 7, the hook mostly stops being a strategic lever and becomes closer to pure housekeeping. A line of -9.5 instead of -10 is still avoiding a technical push at 10 (two touchdowns plus a missed extra point swing, or a field-goal-and-touchdown combination, do occur, just at nowhere near the frequency of 3 or 7), but the difference between betting -9.5 and -10 almost never decides your ticket, because final margins land on 9 or 10 far less often than they land on 3 or 7. If you're deciding where to spend effort shopping for a better half-point across sportsbooks, the two key numbers are where that effort actually pays off most of the time.

Do totals get hooked the same way?

Totals (the combined final score of both teams) get the same push-avoidance treatment, but the underlying math is messier. Combined scores don't cluster around one or two numbers nearly as tightly as single-team margins cluster around 3 and 7, because a total is the sum of two offenses' separate scoring patterns rather than one team's margin over another. That's why you'll still see half-point totals everywhere, but there isn't a widely agreed "key total number" the way there is for spreads — 41, 44, and 47 all show up with roughly similar frequency rather than one number dominating the way 3 and 7 dominate margins. Treat a hooked total as ordinary push-avoidance, not as a signal with the same weight as a hooked spread.

Reading too much into a hook

The most common mistake is treating every half-point as meaningful information about the matchup itself, when most of the time it's simply administrative. A hook on a number nowhere near 3 or 7 is rarely worth obsessing over. The second mistake is ignoring the hook entirely when it does sit at a key number — a bettor who doesn't check whether their line is 2.5, 3, or 3.5 before placing a bet on a game projected to be close is giving up real expected value for no reason, since shopping two or three sportsbooks for the better side of a key-number hook costs nothing and can directly change whether a 3-point loss becomes a push or a loss. Frequently asked questions

Why do sportsbooks avoid whole-number spreads like -3 or -7?

A whole number at a common margin creates the possibility of a push, where the book has to return every dollar wagered on that side without collecting any vig. Adding a half-point ("hooking" the line) makes a push mathematically impossible.

Why are 3 and 7 treated differently from other numbers?

Field goals and touchdowns are the NFL's two scoring plays, so final margins land on exactly 3 or exactly 7 far more often than on most other numbers. That clustering is why sportsbooks and bettors both treat those two numbers as "key numbers."

Is it worth paying extra vig to "buy" half a point off a key number?

It can be, specifically at 3 and, to a lesser degree, 7, because those are the margins most likely to actually change your bet's outcome. Buying a half-point off a non-key number is usually a worse trade, since it's far less likely to matter.

Do totals have a key number the way spreads have 3 and 7?

Not really. Combined final scores are spread across a wider range of numbers than single-team margins are, so no one total number dominates the way 3 and 7 dominate spreads, even though totals still get hooked for the same push-avoidance reasons.

Does a hook tell me which team is going to win?

No. A hook is a push-management and risk-balancing tool for the sportsbook, not a prediction about the final score. It can hint at where betting volume and liability are concentrated, but it isn't a forecast of the outcome.
